stem: A jar contains 11 red candies, 5 yellow candies, and 3 orange candies. If one candy is selected at random, what is the probability of selecting a yellow candy?
explanation: The total number of candies is 11 + 5 + 3 = 19. There are 5 yellow candies, so the probability of selecting a yellow candy is 5/19.

stem: A survey of 180 moviegoers asked about their favorite genre. Of the 82 moviegoers under age 30, 29 preferred comedy. Of the 98 moviegoers aged 30 or older, 42 preferred comedy. If a moviegoer aged 30 or older is selected at random, what is the probability that this person prefers comedy?
explanation: The question asks for the probability that a randomly selected moviegoer aged 30 or older prefers comedy. This is a conditional probability with the condition being aged 30 or older. There are 98 moviegoers aged 30 or older, and 42 of them prefer comedy, so the probability is 42/98, which simplifies to 21/49. The value 42/180 incorrectly uses the total number of moviegoers as the denominator rather than restricting to the 30-or-older group. The value 29/82 gives the probability for the under-30 group instead. The value 42/71 uses an incorrect denominator of 29 + 42 = 71, summing comedy fans across both age groups rather than counting all moviegoers in the 30-or-older group.

stem: A box contains 11 tiles numbered 1 through 11. Two tiles are selected at random without replacement. What is the probability that both tiles show an odd number?
explanation: The odd numbers from 1 through 11 are 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, and 11, giving 6 odd tiles out of 11 total. Since the tiles are drawn without replacement, the probability that the first tile is odd is 6/11, and given that the first tile was odd, the probability that the second tile is also odd is 5/10 = 1/2. Multiplying gives (6/11)(1/2) = 6/22 = 3/11. The value 2/11 results from incorrectly counting only 5 odd numbers and computing (5/11)(4/10) = 20/110 = 2/11. The value 36/121 treats the draws as independent (with replacement), computing (6/11)(6/11). The value 6/11 accounts only for the first draw being odd and ignores the second draw entirely.

skill: Inference from Sample Statistics and Margin of Error
stem: A random sample of 400 registered voters in a city finds that 61% support a proposed park renovation, with a margin of error of 4.1 percentage points. Which of the following is the best interpretation of this result?

options.text: Exactly 61% of all registered voters in the city support the park renovation.
It is plausible that the true percentage of all registered voters in the city who support the park renovation is between 56.9% and 65.1%.
Between 56.9% and 65.1% of the sampled voters support the park renovation.
61% of voters in any city would support the park renovation.

explanation: The margin of error defines a range around the sample statistic within which the true population parameter plausibly lies. Adding and subtracting 4.1 percentage points from 61% gives the interval 56.9% to 65.1%, so it is plausible that the true percentage of all registered voters who support the renovation falls in this range. The claim that exactly 61% of all voters support it ignores sampling variability entirely. The statement about 56.9% to 65.1% of the sampled voters confuses the population inference with a description of the sample itself; the margin of error applies to the population parameter, not the sample. The claim about voters in any city overgeneralizes beyond the population that was sampled.

skill: Inference from Sample Statistics and Margin of Error
stem: A researcher surveys a random sample of 350 residents of a town and finds that 43% support a proposed zoning change, with a margin of error of 4.7 percentage points at a 95% confidence level. Which of the following values is a plausible estimate for the true percentage of all town residents who support the zoning change?
explanation: The confidence interval is 43% minus 4.7 to 43% plus 4.7, which is 38.3% to 47.7%. A plausible value for the true percentage must fall within this interval. The value 39.2% lies within the interval 38.3% to 47.7%, so it is plausible. The value 37.1% falls below the lower bound of 38.3%. The value 48.9% exceeds the upper bound of 47.7%. The value 52.3% is far outside the interval.

skill: Inference from Sample Statistics and Margin of Error
stem: A researcher surveys a random sample of 500 residents from County X and finds that 53% favor a new library, with a margin of error of 4.3 percentage points at 95% confidence. A second researcher surveys a random sample of 500 residents from County Y and finds that 49% favor a new library, with a margin of error of 4.4 percentage points at 95% confidence. Which of the following conclusions is best supported by these results?

options.text: The proportion of residents who favor the library is higher in County X than in County Y.
The proportion who favor the library is exactly 53% in County X and exactly 49% in County Y.
There is not convincing evidence that the proportions who favor the library differ between the two counties.
The results cannot be compared because the surveys were conducted in different counties.

explanation: The confidence interval for County X is 53% minus 4.3 to 53% plus 4.3, or 48.7% to 57.3%. The confidence interval for County Y is 49% minus 4.4 to 49% plus 4.4, or 44.6% to 53.4%. These intervals overlap (from 48.7% to 53.4%), meaning the true proportions could be equal. Because the intervals overlap, there is not convincing evidence that the proportions differ. Claiming the proportion is definitively higher in County X ignores the overlap of the intervals and treats the sample statistics as exact values. Stating the proportions are exactly 53% and 49% confuses sample estimates with population parameters. Claiming the results cannot be compared because they come from different counties is incorrect; comparing results from different populations is a standard and valid statistical practice.

skill: Evaluating Statistical Claims: Observational Studies and Experiments
stem: A school district wants to determine whether a new reading program improves third-grade test scores. The district randomly assigns 150 third-grade students to either the new program or the traditional program and compares their test scores at the end of the year. This study is best described as

options.text: a census
an observational study
a survey
an experiment

explanation: Because the district randomly assigns students to either the new program or the traditional program, treatments are imposed on subjects. This is the defining characteristic of an experiment. A census collects data from every member of a population, which is not what occurred here. An observational study records existing conditions without imposing treatments, but here the programs were assigned by the researcher. A survey collects self-reported data and does not involve assigning treatments.

skill: Evaluating Statistical Claims: Observational Studies and Experiments
stem: A researcher recorded the daily coffee consumption and resting heart rates of 320 adults in a city. She found that adults who drank 4 or more cups of coffee per day had higher average resting heart rates than adults who drank no coffee. The researcher concluded that drinking coffee causes an increase in resting heart rate. Which of the following is the best criticism of this conclusion?

options.text: The sample size of 320 adults is too small to draw any conclusion.
Because participants were not randomly assigned to coffee consumption groups, the difference could be due to other factors.
The researcher should have measured heart rate both before and after coffee consumption.
The conclusion is valid because the sample was large enough to detect a difference.

explanation: This is an observational study because the researcher recorded existing coffee consumption habits rather than assigning participants to drink specific amounts. Without random assignment, confounding variables (such as stress levels, exercise habits, or age) could explain the observed difference in heart rates. Causal conclusions require random assignment to rule out confounders. The claim that 320 adults is too small to draw any conclusion is incorrect; 320 is a reasonable sample size for detecting associations, though sample size does not address the lack of random assignment. Suggesting heart rate should be measured before and after consumption describes a different study design but does not address the fundamental issue that causal claims require random assignment. Asserting the conclusion is valid because the sample is large confuses sample size with study design; a large observational study still cannot establish causation.

skill: Evaluating Statistical Claims: Observational Studies and Experiments
stem: A company wants to determine whether a new training method increases employee productivity. The company randomly selects 90 employees from its 2,400-person workforce and randomly assigns 47 of them to receive the new training and 43 to receive the standard training. After 6 months, the group receiving the new training has a statistically significantly higher average productivity score. Which of the following conclusions is best supported?

options.text: There is an association between the training method and productivity, but a causal relationship cannot be established.
The new training method causes higher productivity among all workers in the industry.
The new training method causes higher productivity among employees at the company.
The new training method would increase productivity at any company of similar size.

explanation: This study has two key design features: random selection from the company's workforce (which allows generalization to all employees at the company) and random assignment to training groups (which allows a causal conclusion). Together, these support the conclusion that the new training method causes higher productivity among employees at the company. The claim that only an association can be established ignores that random assignment was used, which is precisely the mechanism that allows causal inference. The claim about all workers in the industry overgeneralizes beyond the population from which the sample was drawn (the company's own workforce). Similarly, extending the conclusion to any company of similar size goes beyond the sampled population, since employees were selected only from this particular company.
